claim: WASp deficiency is associated with impaired rapamycin-induced autophagosome formation in primary human monocyte-derived macrophages (MDMs).
source: Here, we show that WASp deficiency is associated with impaired rapamycin-induced autophagosome formation and trafficking to lysosomes in primary human monocyte-derived macrophages (MDMs).
evidence: Demonstrated through western blotting showing reduced LC3II expression in WAS KO THP-1 cells and WAS patient MDMs compared to controls following rapamycin treatment, and confocal microscopy showing reduced LC3 punctae formation.

claim: WASp deficiency is associated with impaired trafficking of autophagosomes to lysosomes in primary human MDMs.
source: Here, we show that WASp deficiency is associated with impaired rapamycin-induced autophagosome formation and trafficking to lysosomes in primary human monocyte-derived macrophages (MDMs).
evidence: Demonstrated through confocal microscopy showing disorganized co-localization between LC3 and LAMP-1 in WAS patient MDMs, with scattered punctae rather than perinuclear clustering.

claim: WASp reconstitution in vitro restores autophagic flux in WAS cells.
source: WASp reconstitution in vitro and in WAS patients following clinical gene therapy restores autophagic flux and is dependent on the actin-related protein complex ARP2/3.
evidence: Demonstrated through confocal microscopy showing restoration of LC3 punctae formation in WAS SDMs following lentiviral transduction or gene editing to restore WASp expression.

claim: WASp reconstitution in WAS patients following clinical gene therapy restores autophagic flux.
source: WASp reconstitution in vitro and in WAS patients following clinical gene therapy restores autophagic flux and is dependent on the actin-related protein complex ARP2/3.
evidence: Demonstrated through confocal microscopy showing restoration of LC3 punctae formation in MDMs from WAS patients after gene therapy, comparable to healthy controls.

claim: The role of WASp in autophagic flux is dependent on the actin-related protein complex ARP2/3.
source: WASp reconstitution in vitro and in WAS patients following clinical gene therapy restores autophagic flux and is dependent on the actin-related protein complex ARP2/3.
evidence: Demonstrated through experiments showing that ARP2/3 inhibition with CK666 and ARPC1B deficiency phenocopy WASp deficiency in terms of impaired LC3 punctae formation and LC3-actin association.

claim: Induction of mitochondrial damage with CCCP reveals an ARP2/3-dependent role for WASp in formation of sequestrating actin cages.
source: Induction of mitochondrial damage with CCCP, as a model of selective autophagy, also reveals a novel ARP2/3-dependent role for WASp in formation of sequestrating actin cages and maintenance of mitochondrial network integrity.
evidence: Demonstrated through confocal microscopy showing that healthy donor MDMs form actin cages around damaged mitochondria after CCCP treatment, which is impaired in WAS, CK666-treated, and ARPC1B-deficient MDMs.

claim: WASp plays a role in maintenance of mitochondrial network integrity.
source: Induction of mitochondrial damage with CCCP, as a model of selective autophagy, also reveals a novel ARP2/3-dependent role for WASp in formation of sequestrating actin cages and maintenance of mitochondrial network integrity.
evidence: Demonstrated through confocal microscopy showing that WAS MDMs have predominantly fragmented mitochondria at rest, while healthy donor MDMs have networked mitochondria, and this is restored after gene therapy.

claim: Mitochondrial respiration is suppressed in WAS patient MDMs.
source: Furthermore, mitochondrial respiration is suppressed in WAS patient MDMs and unable to achieve normal maximal activity when stressed, indicating profound intrinsic metabolic dysfunction.
evidence: Demonstrated through Seahorse metabolic flux analysis showing significantly reduced basal mitochondrial respiration (OCR) in WAS MDMs compared to healthy donors.

claim: WAS patient MDMs are unable to achieve normal maximal mitochondrial activity when stressed.
source: Furthermore, mitochondrial respiration is suppressed in WAS patient MDMs and unable to achieve normal maximal activity when stressed, indicating profound intrinsic metabolic dysfunction.
evidence: Demonstrated through Seahorse metabolic flux analysis showing a trend towards reduced maximal respiration in WAS MDMs compared to healthy donors.

claim: WAS patient MDMs exhibit profound intrinsic metabolic dysfunction.
source: Furthermore, mitochondrial respiration is suppressed in WAS patient MDMs and unable to achieve normal maximal activity when stressed, indicating profound intrinsic metabolic dysfunction.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of suppressed basal mitochondrial respiration and inability to achieve normal maximal activity when stressed.

claim: WASp is an essential regulator of the actin cytoskeleton in haematopoietic cells.
source: The Wiskott Aldrich syndrome protein (WASp) is an essential regulator of the actin cytoskeleton in haematopoietic cells.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge cited in the introduction.

claim: WASp co-ordinates cytoskeletal dynamics important in immune cell functions through recruitment of the actin-related protein complex ARP2/3 and formation of new branched actin filaments.
source: It co-ordinates cytoskeletal dynamics important in immune cell functions, through recruitment of the actin-related protein complex ARP2/3 and formation of new branched actin filaments (reviewed in Rivers and Thrasher, 2017).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge from a review article.

claim: Wiskott Aldrich syndrome (WAS) is caused by loss of function of WASp.
source: Wiskott Aldrich syndrome (WAS), caused by loss of function of WASp, is a rare X-linked disorder resulting in significant combined immune deficiency, microthrombocytopaenia and susceptibility to haematological malignancy.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about WAS.

claim: WAS is a rare X-linked disorder.
source: Wiskott Aldrich syndrome (WAS), caused by loss of function of WASp, is a rare X-linked disorder resulting in significant combined immune deficiency, microthrombocytopaenia and susceptibility to haematological malignancy.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about WAS.

claim: WAS results in significant combined immune deficiency.
source: Wiskott Aldrich syndrome (WAS), caused by loss of function of WASp, is a rare X-linked disorder resulting in significant combined immune deficiency, microthrombocytopaenia and susceptibility to haematological malignancy.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about WAS.

claim: WAS results in microthrombocytopaenia.
source: Wiskott Aldrich syndrome (WAS), caused by loss of function of WASp, is a rare X-linked disorder resulting in significant combined immune deficiency, microthrombocytopaenia and susceptibility to haematological malignancy.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about WAS.

claim: WAS results in susceptibility to haematological malignancy.
source: Wiskott Aldrich syndrome (WAS), caused by loss of function of WASp, is a rare X-linked disorder resulting in significant combined immune deficiency, microthrombocytopaenia and susceptibility to haematological malignancy.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about WAS.

claim: Symptoms of classical WAS present in infancy.
source: Symptoms of classical WAS present in infancy and most children will die from disease-related complications in the first 15 years of life, in the absence of definitive treatment by haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) or gene therapy.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about WAS.

claim: Most children with classical WAS will die from disease-related complications in the first 15 years of life in the absence of definitive treatment.
source: Symptoms of classical WAS present in infancy and most children will die from disease-related complications in the first 15 years of life, in the absence of definitive treatment by haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) or gene therapy.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about WAS.

claim: Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) is a definitive treatment for WAS.
source: Symptoms of classical WAS present in infancy and most children will die from disease-related complications in the first 15 years of life, in the absence of definitive treatment by haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) or gene therapy.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about WAS treatment.

claim: Gene therapy is a definitive treatment for WAS.
source: Symptoms of classical WAS present in infancy and most children will die from disease-related complications in the first 15 years of life, in the absence of definitive treatment by haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) or gene therapy.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about WAS treatment.

claim: An inflammatory phenotype occurs in up to 80% of children with WAS.
source: An inflammatory phenotype occurs in up to 80% of children, with symptoms such as severe eczema, inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), arthritis, and vasculitis, which may persist after HSCT in a proportion of children, particularly where myeloid chimerism is low (Worth and Thrasher, 2015).
evidence: This is clinical knowledge from a cited reference.

claim: Inflammatory symptoms in WAS include severe eczema, inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), arthritis, and vasculitis.
source: An inflammatory phenotype occurs in up to 80% of children, with symptoms such as severe eczema, inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), arthritis, and vasculitis, which may persist after HSCT in a proportion of children, particularly where myeloid chimerism is low (Worth and Thrasher, 2015).
evidence: This is clinical knowledge from a cited reference.

claim: Inflammatory symptoms may persist after HSCT in a proportion of WAS children, particularly where myeloid chimerism is low.
source: An inflammatory phenotype occurs in up to 80% of children, with symptoms such as severe eczema, inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), arthritis, and vasculitis, which may persist after HSCT in a proportion of children, particularly where myeloid chimerism is low (Worth and Thrasher, 2015).
evidence: This is clinical knowledge from a cited reference.

claim: Disturbance of the autophagy-inflammasome axis occurs in WASp-deficient murine innate immune cells.
source: We recently demonstrated disturbance of the autophagy-inflammasome axis in WASp-deficient murine innate immune cells (Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study by the authors.

claim: Inflammasomes are cytosolic protein complexes responsible for maturing the pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1β and IL-18.
source: Inflammasomes are cytosolic protein complexes responsible for maturing the pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1β and IL-18 and promoting inflammatory cell death, pyroptosis (Martinon et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge from a cited reference.

claim: Inflammasomes promote inflammatory cell death, pyroptosis.
source: Inflammasomes are cytosolic protein complexes responsible for maturing the pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1β and IL-18 and promoting inflammatory cell death, pyroptosis (Martinon et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge from a cited reference.

claim: Inflammasomes assemble in response to endogenous and/or exogenous danger signals.
source: Assembling in response to endogenous and/or exogenous danger signals, they co-ordinate and aid in mounting appropriate immunity against potential threats, such as from invading pathogens (Guo et al., 2015; Franchi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge from cited references.

claim: Inflammasomes co-ordinate and aid in mounting appropriate immunity against potential threats, such as from invading pathogens.
source: Assembling in response to endogenous and/or exogenous danger signals, they co-ordinate and aid in mounting appropriate immunity against potential threats, such as from invading pathogens (Guo et al., 2015; Franchi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge from cited references.

claim: Autophagy is a lysosomal degradation pathway crucial for maintaining cellular homeostasis.
source: Autophagy is a lysosomal degradation pathway crucial for maintaining cellular homeostasis and downregulating inflammasomes, through clearance of inflammasome triggers (Shi et al., 2012; Harris et al., 2011; Rodgers et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge from cited references.

claim: Autophagy downregulates inflammasomes through clearance of inflammasome triggers.
source: Autophagy is a lysosomal degradation pathway crucial for maintaining cellular homeostasis and downregulating inflammasomes, through clearance of inflammasome triggers (Shi et al., 2012; Harris et al., 2011; Rodgers et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge from cited references.

claim: Autophagosomes are double-membraned vesicles that form around cytoplasmic contents.
source: Autophagosomes are double-membraned vesicles that form around cytoplasmic contents and are transported to lysosomes, where fusion allows for content degradation (Shibutani et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge from a cited reference.

claim: Autophagosomes are transported to lysosomes, where fusion allows for content degradation.
source: Autophagosomes are double-membraned vesicles that form around cytoplasmic contents and are transported to lysosomes, where fusion allows for content degradation (Shibutani et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge from a cited reference.

claim: Autolysosomal contents are recycled either to the cytoplasm, or transported to the cell surface for antigen presentation.
source: Autolysosomal contents are subsequently recycled either to the cytoplasm, or transported to the cell surface for antigen presentation and lysosomes are re-formed ready for further autophagosome interactions (Yu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge from a cited reference.

claim: Lysosomes are re-formed after autolysosomal content degradation, ready for further autophagosome interactions.
source: Autolysosomal contents are subsequently recycled either to the cytoplasm, or transported to the cell surface for antigen presentation and lysosomes are re-formed ready for further autophagosome interactions (Yu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge from a cited reference.

claim: Some autophagic processes are non-selective in nature, such as macroautophagy.
source: Some autophagic processes are non-selective in nature, for example the catabolic degradation of bulk cytoplasmic contents to provide metabolic substrates following nutrient starvation ('macroautophagy').
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about autophagy types.

claim: Macroautophagy involves catabolic degradation of bulk cytoplasmic contents to provide metabolic substrates following nutrient starvation.
source: Some autophagic processes are non-selective in nature, for example the catabolic degradation of bulk cytoplasmic contents to provide metabolic substrates following nutrient starvation ('macroautophagy').
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about macroautophagy.

claim: Some autophagic processes involve selective degradation, such as mitophagy and xenophagy.
source: Others involve selective degradation, for example of damaged organelles, for example mitochondria ('mitophagy') or pathogens that have escaped phagocytosis ('xenophagy').
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about autophagy types.

claim: Mitophagy is the selective degradation of damaged mitochondria.
source: Others involve selective degradation, for example of damaged organelles, for example mitochondria ('mitophagy') or pathogens that have escaped phagocytosis ('xenophagy').
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about mitophagy.

claim: Xenophagy is the selective degradation of pathogens that have escaped phagocytosis.
source: Others involve selective degradation, for example of damaged organelles, for example mitochondria ('mitophagy') or pathogens that have escaped phagocytosis ('xenophagy').
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about xenophagy.

claim: Selective autophagy requires a highly co-ordinated process whereby targets for degradation must first be identified and recruit autophagy receptors.
source: These require a highly co-ordinated process, whereby targets for degradation must first be identified and recruit autophagy receptors.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about selective autophagy.

claim: Actin is involved in autophagy at several levels, including autophagosome formation, maturation, and transport to lysosomes.
source: Actin is involved in autophagy at several levels, including autophagosome formation, maturation, and transport to lysosomes [reviewed in Kast and Dominguez, 2017; Kruppa et al., 2016; Coutts and La Thangue, 2016].
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge from cited review articles.

claim: The ARP2/3 complex has been particularly implicated in autophagy.
source: The ARP2/3 complex, through which WASp acts, consists of seven subunits (ARP2, ARP3 and ARPC1-5) and has been particularly implicated (Kast et al., 2015; Coutts and La Thangue, 2015; Xia et al., 2013; Xia et al., 2014; King et al., 2013; Zavodszky et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge from cited references.

claim: The ARP2/3 complex consists of seven subunits (ARP2, ARP3 and ARPC1-5).
source: The ARP2/3 complex, through which WASp acts, consists of seven subunits (ARP2, ARP3 and ARPC1-5) and has been particularly implicated (Kast et al., 2015; Coutts and La Thangue, 2015; Xia et al., 2013; Xia et al., 2014; King et al., 2013; Zavodszky et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge.

claim: WASp deficiency resulted in the absence of canonical autophagosome formation in an ex vivo model of EPEC infection in murine BMDCs.
source: In an ex vivo model of Enteropathogenic Escherichia coli (EPEC) infection in murine bone-marrow-derived dendritic cells (BMDCs), we provided the first demonstration of a crucial role for WASp in xenophagy, where WASp deficiency resulted in the absence of canonical autophagosome formation (Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study by the authors.

claim: Impaired autophagy in WASp-deficient murine BMDCs contributed to exaggerated inflammasome activity in an EPEC infection model.
source: In this model, impaired autophagy contributed to exaggerated inflammasome activity presumably due to defective clearance of intracellular bacteria.
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study by the authors, with the mechanism being inferred.

claim: Rapamycin inhibits the mTOR complex initiating autophagy.
source: Rapamycin inhibits the mTOR complex initiating autophagy, which culminates in LC3I to LC3II conversion on autophagosome membranes, the latter process being a well-established surrogate marker of autophagosome formation.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about rapamycin's mechanism of action.

claim: LC3I to LC3II conversion on autophagosome membranes is a well-established surrogate marker of autophagosome formation.
source: Rapamycin inhibits the mTOR complex initiating autophagy, which culminates in LC3I to LC3II conversion on autophagosome membranes, the latter process being a well-established surrogate marker of autophagosome formation.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about LC3 as a marker.

claim: In WT THP-1 cells, an increase in LC3II expression was observed following rapamycin exposure.
source: In WT THP-1 cells, an increase in LC3II expression was observed (Figure 1a).
evidence: Demonstrated through western blotting shown in Figure 1a.

claim: LC3II expression did not increase in WAS KO THP-1 cells following rapamycin exposure.
source: In contrast, LC3II expression did not increase in the absence of WASp, leading to a significant reduction in LC3II expression in WAS KO compared with WT cells (Figure 1a and b).
evidence: Demonstrated through western blotting shown in Figure 1a and quantified in Figure 1b.

claim: Bafilomycin inhibits autophagosome-lysosome fusion, preventing lysosomal degradation of autophagosomes.
source: Bafilomycin inhibits autophagosome-lysosome fusion, preventing lysosomal degradation of autophagosomes.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about bafilomycin's mechanism of action.

claim: Co-culture with rapamycin and bafilomycin confirmed that reduced LC3II expression in WAS KO THP-1 cells was indicative of impaired autophagosome formation rather than increased degradation.
source: Co-culture with the combination of rapamycin and bafilomycin confirmed that reduced LC3II expression observed in WAS KO THP-1 cells was indicative of impaired autophagosome formation rather than increased degradation (Figure 1a).
evidence: Demonstrated through western blotting shown in Figure 1a using bafilomycin to block degradation.

claim: Reduced LC3II expression in WAS KO THP-1 cells was confirmed in primary human MDMs derived from a WAS patient compared with a healthy donor.
source: This observation was confirmed in primary human monocyte-derived macrophages (MDMs) derived from a WAS patient compared with a healthy donor (Figure 1c and d).
evidence: Demonstrated through western blotting shown in Figure 1c and quantified in Figure 1d.

claim: The increase in LC3II expression in response to rapamycin/bafilomycin treatment in healthy donor MDMs correlated with an increase in LC3 punctae in the perinuclear region.
source: Confocal microscopic analysis of healthy donor MDMs demonstrated that the increase in LC3II expression in response to rapamycin/bafilomycin treatment correlated with an increase in LC3 punctae in the perinuclear region (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d and e).
evidence: Demonstrated through confocal microscopy shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d and e.

claim: LC3 punctae in healthy donor MDMs represent autophagosomes that gather around the centrosomes.
source: Further analysis by electron microscopy (EM) revealed that these LC3 punctae represent autophagosomes, which gather around the centrosomes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: Demonstrated through electron microscopy shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1f.

claim: WAS SDMs and MDMs showed significant reduction in LC3 punctae formation compared with healthy donors following rapamycin/bafilomycin treatment.
source: WAS SDMs and MDMs showed significant reduction in LC3 punctae formation when compared with healthy donors (Figure 1e–h), supporting the hypothesis that autophagosome formation is indeed impaired in the absence of WASp.
evidence: Demonstrated through confocal microscopy shown in Figure 1e-h.

claim: WAS-corrected SDMs demonstrated significantly greater LC3 punctae formation compared with uncorrected SDMs from the same WAS patients following rapamycin-induced autophagy.
source: Rapamycin-induced autophagy of these WAS-corrected SDMs demonstrated significantly greater LC3 punctae formation compared with uncorrected SDMs from the same WAS patients (Figure 1e and f).
evidence: Demonstrated through confocal microscopy shown in Figure 1e and quantified in Figure 1f.

claim: Rapamycin stimulation of MDMs from WAS patients treated with gene therapy demonstrated LC3 punctae formation comparable to healthy controls.
source: These findings were confirmed following in vivo WASp reconstitution in WAS patients treated with clinical gene therapy, where rapamycin stimulation of MDMs from WAS patients treated with gene therapy demonstrated LC3 punctae formation comparable to healthy controls (Figure 1g and h).
evidence: Demonstrated through confocal microscopy shown in Figure 1g and quantified in Figure 1h.

claim: Restoration of LC3 punctae was observed in MDMs from the same WAS patient at 6 and 9 months after engraftment of corrected HSPCs following gene therapy.
source: Additionally, we were able to follow one patient through gene therapy, repeating rapamycin stimulation of MDMs from the same patient before and after treatment, with restoration of LC3 punctae observed at 6 and 9 months after engraftment of corrected HSPCs (Figure 1i).
evidence: Demonstrated through confocal microscopy shown in Figure 1i.

claim: The cellular location of LC3 punctae in WAS SDMs and MDMs differed when compared with healthy donors, being scattered throughout the cytoplasm instead of perinuclear clustering.
source: In addition to reduced number, the cellular location of the LC3 punctae in WAS SDMs and MDMs differed when compared with heathy donors. Instead of peninuclear clustering, LC3 punctae in WAS SDMs and MDMs were scattered throughout the cytoplasm (Figure 1e and g).
evidence: Observed through confocal microscopy shown in Figure 1e and g.

claim: In resting healthy donor MDMs, few LC3 punctae were seen scattered throughout the cytoplasm.
source: In resting healthy donor MDMs, few LC3 punctae were seen scattered throughout the cytoplasm (Figure 2a).
evidence: Observed through confocal microscopy shown in Figure 2a.

claim: LAMP-1 staining showed that lysosomes are more plentiful and found predominantly in the perinuclear region at rest in healthy donor MDMs.
source: In contrast, LAMP-1 staining showed that lysosomes are more plentiful and found predominantly in the perinuclear region at rest.
evidence: Observed through confocal microscopy shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Upon rapamycin-induced autophagy in healthy donor MDMs, LC3 punctae markedly increased in number and co-localised with LAMP-1 punctae in the perinuclear region.
source: Upon rapamycin-induced autophagy, LC3 punctae markedly increased in number and co-localised with LAMP-1 punctae in the perinuclear region.
evidence: Observed through confocal microscopy shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Co-localisation of LC3 and LAMP-1 in the perinuclear region of healthy donor MDMs was around the microtubule organising centres.
source: EM analysis revealed that this co-localisation in the perinuclear region was around the microtubule organising centres (Figure 1—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: Demonstrated through electron microscopy shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1f.

claim: Autophagosomes are formed in the cytoplasm and travel along microtubules for lysosomal fusion.
source: Taken together, the data suggest that autophagosomes are formed in the cytoplasm and travel along microtubules for lysosomal fusion.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that LC3 punctae increase in the cytoplasm and then co-localize with LAMP-1 in the perinuclear region around microtubule organizing centers.

claim: WAS patient MDMs revealed disorganised co-localisation between LC3 and LAMP-1, with more than one cluster of LC3 and LAMP-1 punctae in addition to uncoordinated punctae scattered throughout the cytoplasm.
source: In contrast to healthy donors, WAS patient MDMs revealed disorganised co-localisation between LC3 and LAMP-1, with more than one cluster of LC3 and LAMP-1 punctae in addition to uncoordinated punctae scattered throughout the cytoplasm (Figure 2a).
evidence: Observed through confocal microscopy shown in Figure 2a.

claim: A significant reduction in LAMP-1 punctae was noted in WAS patient MDMs compared with healthy donors, both at rest and following autophagy stimulation.
source: It is important to note that in addition to disrupted LC3 and LAMP-1 punctae co-ordination, a significant reduction in LAMP-1 punctae was noted in WAS patient MDMs compared with healthy donors, both at rest and following autophagy stimulation.
evidence: Observed through confocal microscopy shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Reduced protein expression of LAMP-1 was confirmed in WASp-deficient THP-1 cells and primary MDMs.
source: This was confirmed by reduced protein expression of LAMP-1 in WASp-deficient THP-1 cells and primary MDMs (Figure 2b–e).
evidence: Demonstrated through western blotting shown in Figure 2b-e.

claim: An abundance of single-membraned tubular structures was observed in healthy donor MDMs by EM analysis.
source: Through EM analysis, we observed an abundance of single-membraned tubular structures in healthy donor MDMs, which were surprisingly reduced in WAS patient MDMs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Observed through electron microscopy shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Single-membraned tubular structures were reduced in WAS patient MDMs compared to healthy donor MDMs.
source: Through EM analysis, we observed an abundance of single-membraned tubular structures in healthy donor MDMs, which were surprisingly reduced in WAS patient MDMs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Observed through electron microscopy shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Tubular lysosomes have previously been reported in macrophages.
source: Although tubular lysosomes have previously been reported in macrophages (Swanson et al., 1987), without further staining it is difficult to say with confidence whether these tubular structures represent lysosomes or not.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge from a cited reference.

claim: Reduced LAMP-1 in WAS could indicate a potential role for WASp in lysosome formation.
source: Collectively, these observations could indicate a potential role for WASp in lysosome formation, or a reduction in basal autophagic flux in WAS, since an important source of lysosomes is from recycling of material from autophagolysosomes.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation of reduced LAMP-1 in WAS cells.

claim: Reduced LAMP-1 in WAS could indicate a reduction in basal autophagic flux in WAS.
source: Collectively, these observations could indicate a potential role for WASp in lysosome formation, or a reduction in basal autophagic flux in WAS, since an important source of lysosomes is from recycling of material from autophagolysosomes.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation of reduced LAMP-1 in WAS cells and knowledge that lysosomes are recycled from autophagolysosomes.

claim: Confocal analysis of healthy donor MDMs and SDMs exposed to rapamycin demonstrated close association of actin with LC3.
source: Confocal analysis of healthy donor MDMs and SDMs exposed to rapamycin demonstrated close association of actin with LC3 (Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Observed through confocal microscopy shown in Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Deconvolution of super resolution confocal images revealed true co-localisation with actin rings directly overlapping rings of LC3 in some instances.
source: More detailed analysis using deconvolution of super resolution confocal images revealed that in some instances there was also true co-localisation, with actin rings directly overlapping rings of LC3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a and b).
evidence: Observed through super resolution confocal microscopy shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a and b.

claim: Actin localisation with LC3 was impaired in WAS patient MDMs and SDMs.
source: Actin localisation with LC3 was impaired in WAS patient MDMs (Figure 3a and b) and SDMs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c), but restored following WASp reconstitution either in vitro (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c) or in vivo (Figure 3a and b), suggesting that the role of WASp in these cellular processes is largely actin-dependent.
evidence: Observed through confocal microscopy shown in Figure 3a, b, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Actin-LC3 association was restored following WASp reconstitution either in vitro or in vivo.
source: Actin localisation with LC3 was impaired in WAS patient MDMs (Figure 3a and b) and SDMs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c), but restored following WASp reconstitution either in vitro (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c) or in vivo (Figure 3a and b), suggesting that the role of WASp in these cellular processes is largely actin-dependent.
evidence: Observed through confocal microscopy shown in Figure 3a, b, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1c.

claim: The role of WASp in non-selective autophagy is largely actin-dependent.
source: Actin localisation with LC3 was impaired in WAS patient MDMs (Figure 3a and b) and SDMs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c), but restored following WASp reconstitution either in vitro (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c) or in vivo (Figure 3a and b), suggesting that the role of WASp in these cellular processes is largely actin-dependent.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that actin-LC3 association is impaired in WAS and restored upon WASp reconstitution.

claim: Healthy donor MDMs treated with CK666 prior to rapamycin treatment lost their ability to form LC3 punctae, recapitulating WASp-deficiency.
source: Healthy donor MDMs treated with CK666 (a chemical inhibitor of ARP2/3 complex activity), prior to rapamycin treatment, lost their ability to form LC3 punctae, strikingly recapitulating WASp-deficiency (Figure 3c and d).
evidence: Observed through confocal microscopy shown in Figure 3c and quantified in Figure 3d.

claim: ARPC1B is one of the seven subunits comprising the ARP2/3 complex.
source: ARPC1B is one of the seven subunits comprising the ARP2/3 complex.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge.

claim: Patients with defects in ARPC1B exhibit a clinical phenotype largely similar to WAS.
source: Patients with defects in this subunit exhibit a clinical phenotype largely similar to WAS (Kahr et al., 2017; Kopitar et al., 2019), suggesting the two conditions share underlying mechanism(s).
evidence: This is clinical knowledge from cited references.

claim: WAS and ARPC1B deficiency share underlying mechanism(s).
source: Patients with defects in this subunit exhibit a clinical phenotype largely similar to WAS (Kahr et al., 2017; Kopitar et al., 2019), suggesting the two conditions share underlying mechanism(s).
evidence: Inferred from the similarity in clinical phenotypes between WAS and ARPC1B deficiency.

claim: Primary MDMs from ARPC1B-deficient patients were unable to form podosomes.
source: Primary MDMs from ARPC1B-deficient patients were also unable to form podosomes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: Observed through confocal microscopy shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Induction of non-selective autophagy in ARPC1B-deficient MDMs resulted in impaired LC3 punctae formation.
source: Furthermore, induction of non-selective autophagy in ARPC1B-deficient MDMs resulted in impaired LC3 punctae formation (Figure 3c and d), LC3-actin association (Figure 3b), and LC3II expression (Figure 3e and f), as seen in WAS.
evidence: Observed through confocal microscopy shown in Figure 3c and d.

claim: Induction of non-selective autophagy in ARPC1B-deficient MDMs resulted in impaired LC3-actin association.
source: Furthermore, induction of non-selective autophagy in ARPC1B-deficient MDMs resulted in impaired LC3 punctae formation (Figure 3c and d), LC3-actin association (Figure 3b), and LC3II expression (Figure 3e and f), as seen in WAS.
evidence: Observed through confocal microscopy shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Induction of non-selective autophagy in ARPC1B-deficient MDMs resulted in impaired LC3II expression.
source: Furthermore, induction of non-selective autophagy in ARPC1B-deficient MDMs resulted in impaired LC3 punctae formation (Figure 3c and d), LC3-actin association (Figure 3b), and LC3II expression (Figure 3e and f), as seen in WAS.
evidence: Demonstrated through western blotting shown in Figure 3e and quantified in Figure 3f.

claim: During non-selective autophagy in human MDMs and SDMs, actin associates with LC3 punctae in a WASp and ARP2/3-dependent manner.
source: Taken together, our observations suggest that during non-selective autophagy in human MDMs and SDMs, actin associates with LC3 punctae in a WASp and ARP2/3-dependent manner.
evidence: Inferred from the collective observations that actin-LC3 association is impaired in WAS, CK666-treated, and ARPC1B-deficient cells.

claim: Analysis of WASp's amino acid sequence did not find any xLIR domains.
source: Analysis of WASp's amino acid sequence did not find any xLIR domains (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Determined through bioinformatic analysis using the iLIR web resource platform.

claim: Several WxxL motifs were identified in WASp, but similarity scores (PSSM scores) were low (max. 10), making a functional interaction between WASp and LC3 unlikely.
source: Several WxxL motifs were identified, but similarity scores (PSSM scores) were low (max. 10), making a functional interaction between WASp and LC3 unlikely.
evidence: Determined through bioinformatic analysis using the iLIR web resource platform.

claim: ARPC1B was identified to have a WxxL motif with high PSSM score that could be predicted to contain a functional LIR motif.
source: Additionally, ARPC1B was identified to have a WxxL motif with high PSSM score that could also be predicted to contain a functional LIR motif.
evidence: Determined through bioinformatic analysis using the iLIR web resource platform.

claim: CCCP is routinely employed to investigate mitophagy.
source: The protonophore carbonyl cyanide 3-chlorophenylhydrazone (CCCP) is routinely employed to investigate mitophagy (Kruppa et al., 2018; Villa et al., 2017; Hsieh and Yang, 2019).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge from cited references.

claim: CCCP treatment results in depolarization of the mitochondrial membrane and fragmentation of the mitochondrial network.
source: By depolarising the mitochondrial membrane, CCCP treatment results in fragmentation of the mitochondrial network (without causing cell death; Figure 4—figure supplement 1b), with damaged mitochondria being targeted for degradation by mitophagy.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge, with cell viability data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b.

claim: CCCP treatment does not cause cell death in MDMs.
source: By depolarising the mitochondrial membrane, CCCP treatment results in fragmentation of the mitochondrial network (without causing cell death; Figure 4—figure supplement 1b), with damaged mitochondria being targeted for degradation by mitophagy.
evidence: Demonstrated through flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Following CCCP treatment, healthy donor MDMs demonstrated marked disruption of the mitochondrial network.
source: Following CCCP treatment, healthy donor MDMs demonstrated marked disruption of the mitochondrial network (Figure 4a).
evidence: Observed through confocal microscopy shown in Figure 4a.

claim: When bafilomycin was used in combination with CCCP treatment in healthy donor MDMs, clusters of mitochondria were found to be surrounded by actin cages.
source: When bafilomycin was used in combination with CCCP treatment (to prevent mitophagosome degradation), clusters of mitochondria were found to be surrounded by actin cages, suggesting successful identification of damaged mitochondria and isolation from the healthy network.
evidence: Observed through confocal microscopy shown in Figure 4a.

claim: In some instances following CCCP/bafilomycin treatment of healthy donor MDMs, the mitochondrial network was completely disrupted, with only fragments of mitochondria visible within actin cages.
source: In some instances, the network was completely disrupted, with only fragments of mitochondria visible within actin cages (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Observed through confocal microscopy shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Localisation of LC3 to actin cages confirms that encapsulated mitochondria were targeted for degradation by mitophagy.
source: Localisation of LC3 to these actin cages confirms that encapsulated mitochondria were targeted for degradation by mitophagy.
evidence: Observed through confocal microscopy shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: WAS MDMs demonstrated a lack of mitochondrial clustering following CCCP treatment.
source: In marked contrast to healthy donors, WAS MDMs demonstrated a lack of mitochondrial clustering, with significantly impaired actin cage formation (Figure 4a and b).
evidence: Observed through confocal microscopy shown in Figure 4a and quantified in Figure 4b.

claim: WAS MDMs demonstrated significantly impaired actin cage formation following CCCP treatment.
source: In marked contrast to healthy donors, WAS MDMs demonstrated a lack of mitochondrial clustering, with significantly impaired actin cage formation (Figure 4a and b).
evidence: Observed through confocal microscopy shown in Figure 4a and quantified in Figure 4b.

claim: Where actin cages were present in WAS MDMs following CCCP treatment, they were small and demonstrated reduced LC3 recruitment.
source: Where present, actin cages were small and demonstrated reduced LC3 recruitment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a and c).
evidence: Observed through confocal microscopy shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a and quantified in Figure 4—figure supplement 1c.

claim: In vivo WAS correction through clinical gene therapy restored mitophagy.
source: In vivo WAS correction, through clinical gene therapy, restored mitophagy (Figure 4a and b), indicating that the formation of actin cages around damaged mitochondria is a WASp-dependent process.
evidence: Observed through confocal microscopy shown in Figure 4a and quantified in Figure 4b.

claim: The formation of actin cages around damaged mitochondria is a WASp-dependent process.
source: In vivo WAS correction, through clinical gene therapy, restored mitophagy (Figure 4a and b), indicating that the formation of actin cages around damaged mitochondria is a WASp-dependent process.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that actin cage formation is impaired in WAS and restored after gene therapy.

claim: Inhibiting ARP2/3 activity of healthy donor MDMs led to significant disruption of actin cage formation after induction of mitochondrial damage.
source: Furthermore, inhibiting ARP2/3 activity of healthy donor MDMs led to significant disruption of actin cage formation after induction of mitochondrial damage.
evidence: Observed through confocal microscopy shown in Figure 4b and c.

claim: Mitophagy induction in primary ARPC1B-deficient MDMs revealed impaired actin cage formation.
source: Similarly, mitophagy induction in primary ARPC1B-deficient MDMs revealed impaired actin cage formation, thereby mimicking the WASp-deficient phenotype (Figure 4b and c).
evidence: Observed through confocal microscopy shown in Figure 4b and c.

claim: Human WASp plays an important role in mitophagy, which is dependent on activation of the ARP2/3 complex.
source: In summary, the present study provides the first evidence of an important role for human WASp in mitophagy, which is dependent on activation of the ARP2/3 complex.
evidence: Inferred from the collective observations that mitophagy is impaired in WAS, CK666-treated, and ARPC1B-deficient cells.

claim: Mitophagy is integral to mitochondrial homeostasis.
source: Mitophagy is integral to mitochondrial homeostasis and increasing evidence suggests that actin is crucial for mitochondrial fission and fusion (Li et al., 2015; Hatch et al., 2014; Moore et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge from cited references.

claim: Increasing evidence suggests that actin is crucial for mitochondrial fission and fusion.
source: Mitophagy is integral to mitochondrial homeostasis and increasing evidence suggests that actin is crucial for mitochondrial fission and fusion (Li et al., 2015; Hatch et al., 2014; Moore et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge from cited references.

claim: At rest, healthy donor MDMs demonstrated two main categories of mitochondrial morphology: networked and fragmented.
source: At rest, healthy donor MDMs demonstrated two main categories of mitochondrial morphology:networked and fragmented (Figure 5a).
evidence: Observed through confocal microscopy shown in Figure 5a.

claim: In the majority of healthy donor MDMs, mitochondria existed in networks, with a small percentage of fragmented morphology.
source: In the majority, mitochondria existed in networks, with a small percentage of fragmented morphology (Figure 5b and c).
evidence: Observed through confocal microscopy shown in Figure 5b and quantified in Figure 5c.

claim: Mitochondrial networks in healthy donor MDMs are present at the basal cell surface, with actin foci consistent with podosomes observed in close proximity.
source: Co-staining for f-actin revealed the presence of these networks at the basal cell surface, with actin foci, consistent with podosomes, observed in close proximity.
evidence: Observed through confocal microscopy shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The majority of mitochondria in WAS MDMs were fragmented at rest.
source: Unlike healthy donors, the majority of mitochondria in WAS MDMs were fragmented and where networks were present, these were found throughout the cell cytoplasm rather than at the basal cell surface (Figure 5b and c).
evidence: Observed through confocal microscopy shown in Figure 5b and quantified in Figure 5c.

claim: Where mitochondrial networks were present in WAS MDMs, these were found throughout the cell cytoplasm rather than at the basal cell surface.
source: Unlike healthy donors, the majority of mitochondria in WAS MDMs were fragmented and where networks were present, these were found throughout the cell cytoplasm rather than at the basal cell surface (Figure 5b and c).
evidence: Observed through confocal microscopy shown in Figure 5b and quantified in Figure 5c.

claim: After gene therapy, the basal mitochondrial morphology of corrected WAS MDMs returned to a prominent basal location, akin to healthy controls.
source: After gene therapy, the basal mitochondrial morphology of corrected WAS MDMs returned to a prominent basal location, akin to healthy controls (Figure 5b and c).
evidence: Observed through confocal microscopy shown in Figure 5b and quantified in Figure 5c.

claim: Even in the absence of additional mitochondrial insult, basal mitochondrial homeostasis is compromised in WAS.
source: This suggests that, even in the absence of additional mitochondrial insult, basal mitochondrial homeostasis is compromised.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that WAS MDMs have predominantly fragmented mitochondria at rest.

claim: WASp may play a vital role in maintenance of a healthy mitochondrial network.
source: This is a significant finding as it suggests for the first time that WASp may play a vital role in maintenance of a healthy mitochondrial network.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that WAS MDMs have disrupted mitochondrial morphology at rest, which is restored after gene therapy.

claim: Inhibition of ARP2/3 in healthy donor MDMs with CK666 led to fragmentation of mitochondrial networks, sharing the WAS phenotype.
source: Inhibition of ARP2/3 in healthy donor MDMs with CK666 led to fragmentation of mitochondrial networks, sharing the WAS phenotype.
evidence: Observed through confocal microscopy shown in Figure 5c and d.

claim: Basal mitochondrial morphology of ARPC1B-deficient MDMs was disrupted.
source: Basal mitochondrial morphology of ARPC1B-deficient MDMs was also disrupted, but subtle differences were noted.
evidence: Observed through confocal microscopy shown in Figure 5c and d.

claim: A reduction of networked mitochondria was seen in ARPC1B-deficient MDMs compared with healthy donor MDMs, but this did not reach statistical significance.
source: As with WAS and CK666-treated MDMs, a reduction of networked mitochondria was seen in ARPC1B-deficient MDMs, compared with healthy donor MDMs; however, this did not reach statistical significance.
evidence: Observed through confocal microscopy shown in Figure 5c and d.

claim: The morphology of networked mitochondria in ARPC1B-deficient MDMs appeared more elongated compared with healthy donor MDMs.
source: Interestingly, however, the morphology of networked mitochondria in ARPC1B-deficient MDMs appeared more elongated compared with healthy donor MDMs (Figure 5d).
evidence: Observed through confocal microscopy shown in Figure 5d.

claim: ARPC1B may play a specific role in mitochondrial fission, through WASp-independent pathways.
source: The functional significance of this observation is at present unknown, but it is tempting to speculate that ARPC1B may play a specific role in mitochondrial fission, through WASp-independent pathways.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation of elongated mitochondria in ARPC1B-deficient MDMs.

claim: WASp plays a crucial role in maintenance of mitochondrial homeostasis, which is also ARP2/3-dependent.
source: Collectively, our observations provide novel evidence that WASp plays a crucial role in maintenance of mitochondrial homeostasis, which is also ARP2/3-dependent.
evidence: Inferred from the collective observations that mitochondrial morphology is disrupted in WAS, CK666-treated, and ARPC1B-deficient cells.

claim: WAS MDMs exhibited significant reduction in basal mitochondrial respiration.
source: In these experiments, WAS MDMs exhibited significant reduction in basal mitochondrial respiration and trend towards reduced maximal respiration (Figure 6a and b).
evidence: Demonstrated through Seahorse metabolic flux analysis shown in Figure 6a and quantified in Figure 6b.

claim: WAS MDMs exhibited a trend towards reduced maximal respiration.
source: In these experiments, WAS MDMs exhibited significant reduction in basal mitochondrial respiration and trend towards reduced maximal respiration (Figure 6a and b).
evidence: Demonstrated through Seahorse metabolic flux analysis shown in Figure 6a and quantified in Figure 6b.

claim: Concomitant analysis of extracellular acidification rates (ECAR) found no significant difference between healthy donor and WAS MDMs.
source: Concomitant analysis of extracellular acidification rates (ECAR), reflecting aerobic glycolysis, found no significant difference between healthy donor and WAS MDMs (Figure 6c and d), suggesting no compensatory switch to aerobic glycolysis as described for other cell types in the absence of autophagy (Clarke and Simon, 2019).
evidence: Demonstrated through Seahorse metabolic flux analysis shown in Figure 6c and quantified in Figure 6d.

claim: There is no compensatory switch to aerobic glycolysis in WAS MDMs.
source: Concomitant analysis of extracellular acidification rates (ECAR), reflecting aerobic glycolysis, found no significant difference between healthy donor and WAS MDMs (Figure 6c and d), suggesting no compensatory switch to aerobic glycolysis as described for other cell types in the absence of autophagy (Clarke and Simon, 2019).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that ECAR is not increased in WAS MDMs despite reduced OxPhos.

claim: The inability of WAS MDMs to respond to impaired OxPhos by upregulating aerobic glycolysis raises the possibility that metabolic undersupply could lead to downstream functional cellular consequences.
source: The inability of WAS MDMs to respond to impaired OxPhos by upregulating aerobic glycolysis raises the possibility that metabolic undersupply could lead to downstream functional cellular consequences.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that WAS MDMs have reduced OxPhos without compensatory increase in glycolysis.

claim: The potential role of WASp in both non-selective autophagy and selective mitophagy in human myeloid cells was investigated in the present study.
source: In the present study, the potential contribution of WASp to both non-selective autophagy and selective mitophagy in human myeloid cells was investigated.
evidence: This is a statement of the study's objectives.

claim: A significant role for human WASp in autophagosome formation and dynamics was uncovered.
source: A significant role for human WASp in autophagosome formation and dynamics was uncovered.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: WASp-deficiency resulted in only modest reduction in LC3II expression in THP-1 and primary MDMs.
source: Although WASp-deficiency resulted in only modest reduction in LC3II expression in THP-1 and primary MDMs, this is in keeping with our previous findings in murine BMDCs following rapamycin-induced autophagy (Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings and comparison to previous work.

claim: In xenophagy, modest reduction in LC3II expression correlated with complete absence of canonical autophagosome formation around intracellular bacteria.
source: Importantly, in xenophagy, our previous work demonstrated that this same modest reduction in LC3II expression correlated with complete absence of canonical autophagosome formation around intracellular bacteria (Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study by the authors.

claim: Expression of LC3II is not exclusive to mature autophagosomes, but may also associate with immature autophagosomes and other single-membraned vesicles.
source: This finding highlights that expression of LC3II is not exclusive to mature autophagosomes, but may also associate with immature autophagosomes and other single-membraned vesicles.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings from the current and previous studies.

claim: Reduced LC3II expression in THP-1 cells and primary WAS MDMs correlates with a significant reduction in LC3 punctae.
source: Here, we show that reduced LC3II expression in THP-1 cells and primary WAS MDMs correlates with a significant reduction in LC3 punctae, a surrogate marker for autophagosome formation, which are restored following in vitro and in vivo WAS correction.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: The mechanism of human WASp action in non-selective autophagy and mitophagy is dependent on ARP2/3-mediated actin polymerisation.
source: In the present study, we elucidated that the mechanism of human WASp action in non-selective autophagy and mitophagy is dependent on ARP2/3-mediated actin polymerisation.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: Actin is seen to colocalise with LC3 punctae in rapamycin-induced autophagy of healthy donor SDMs and MDMs, which is abrogated in WAS, ARP2/3-inhibited healthy donors and ARPC1B-deficient patients.
source: Actin is seen to colocalise with LC3 punctae in rapamycin-induced autophagy of healthy donor SDMs and MDMs, which is abrogated in WAS, ARP2/3-inhibited healthy donors and ARPC1B-deficient patients.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: Restoration of actin-LC3 punctae association following in vitro and in vivo WAS correction confirms a WASp-dependent role in non-selective autophagy.
source: Restoration of actin-LC3 punctae association following in vitro and in vivo WAS correction confirms a WASp-dependent role in this model.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: Identification of potential LIR motifs in ARP2/3 components, not present in WASp, adds further support to the notion that the role of WASp in autophagy is via ARP2/3 actin polymerisation.
source: Identification of potential LIR motifs in ARP2/3 components, not present in WASp, adds further support to the notion that the role of WASp in autophagy is via ARP2/3 actin polymerisation; however, it is worth also noting that LIR-independent modes of interaction with Atg-8 family proteins have also been reported (Behrends et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the bioinformatic analysis findings.

claim: LIR-independent modes of interaction with Atg-8 family proteins have been reported.
source: Identification of potential LIR motifs in ARP2/3 components, not present in WASp, adds further support to the notion that the role of WASp in autophagy is via ARP2/3 actin polymerisation; however, it is worth also noting that LIR-independent modes of interaction with Atg-8 family proteins have also been reported (Behrends et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge from a cited reference.

claim: Impaired autophagy in ARP2/3-inhibited and ARPC1B-deficient patients highlights a potential WASp-independent role for ARP2/3 in autophagy.
source: Impaired autophagy in ARP2/3-inhibited and ARPC1B-deficient patients, also highlight a potential WASp-independent role for ARP2/3 in autophagy.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Reduction in LC3II protein expression following rapamycin-induced autophagy of ARPC1B-deficient patients was more profound than that seen in WAS.
source: Interestingly, reduction in LC3II protein expression following rapamycin-induced autophagy of ARPC1B-deficient patients, compared with healthy donors, was more profound than that seen in WAS.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: The more profound reduction in LC3II in ARPC1B deficiency may reflect WASp-independent polymerisation of actin via the ARP2/3 complex.
source: This may reflect WASp-independent polymerisation of actin via the ARP2/3 complex, which may be of particular importance in potential for compensatory mechanisms to restore some autophagic activity essential for cell survival in WASp deficiency.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that ARPC1B deficiency has a more severe autophagy defect than WAS.

claim: The transport of mature autophagosomes to lysosomes in non-haematopoietic cell lines relies on microtubules.
source: In addition to the role of actin in autophagosome formation and dynamics, existing evidence demonstrates that the transport of mature autophagosomes to lysosomes in non-haematopoietic cell lines relies on microtubules (Jahreiss et al., 2008; Kimura et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge from cited references.

claim: EM and confocal analyses of primary MDMs following rapamycin-induced autophagy identified clustering of autophagosomes around microtubule-organising centres.
source: Our EM and confocal analyses of primary MDMs following rapamycin-induced autophagy identified clustering of autophagosomes around microtubule-organising centres.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: In autophagy there may be a direct role of WASp in microtubule-dependent trafficking of autophagosomes.
source: Although previous evidence to support a role of WASp in microtubule homeostasis is limited predominantly to a study where WASp was overexpressed in Cos7 cells (Tian et al., 2000), our data suggests in autophagy there may be a direct role of WASp in microtubule-dependent trafficking of autophagosomes.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation of disrupted autophagosome trafficking in WAS and previous limited evidence of WASp's role in microtubules.

claim: There appeared to be a reduction in lysosome numbers in untreated WAS MDMs.
source: We were surprised to note that there appeared to be a reduction in lysosome numbers in untreated WAS MDMs.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: Reduced lysosomes in WAS could indicate an additional role for WASp in lysosome formation.
source: This could indicate an additional role for WASp in lysosome formation, or reflect impaired basal autophagic flux, since lysosomes re-form in late autophagy following content degradation of the autophagolysosomes (Yu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation of reduced lysosomes in WAS.

claim: Reduced lysosomes in WAS may be important in antigen presentation.
source: Functionally, this observation may be important in antigen presentation, a role previously described for lysosomes in macrophages (Vyas et al., 2007; Saric et al., 2016).
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation of reduced lysosomes in WAS and established knowledge of lysosome function.

claim: Mitochondria are essential in providing energy for cellular homeostasis.
source: Mitochondria are essential in providing energy for cellular homeostasis and play an important role in innate immunity, contributing to pathogen control through bactericidal activity of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS) (West et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge from a cited reference.

claim: Mitochondria play an important role in innate immunity, contributing to pathogen control through bactericidal activity of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS).
source: Mitochondria are essential in providing energy for cellular homeostasis and play an important role in innate immunity, contributing to pathogen control through bactericidal activity of mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mtROS) (West et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge from a cited reference.

claim: ROS can lead to damage of cellular organelles, including the mitochondria themselves.
source: However, ROS can also lead to damage of cellular organelles, including the mitochondria themselves.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge.

claim: Mitophagy plays a crucial role in ensuring damaged mitochondria are effectively cleared in order to maintain mitochondrial network integrity and cellular homeostasis.
source: Mitophagy plays a crucial role in ensuring damaged mitochondria are effectively cleared in order to maintain mitochondrial network integrity and cellular homeostasis.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge.

claim: Sites of actin polymerisation surrounding mitochondria that had become detached from the mitochondrial network were found in a model of CCCP-induced mitophagy of primary MDMs, encapsulating them in cage-like structures.
source: In a model of CCCP-induced mitophagy of primary MDMs, we found sites of actin polymerisation surrounding mitochondria that had become detached from the mitochondrial network, encapsulating them in cage-like structures.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: Actin-cage formation around damaged mitochondria was abrogated in WAS, ARP2/3-inhibited and ARPC1B-deficient patient MDMs and restored in WAS patients after clinical gene therapy.
source: Actin-cage formation around damaged mitochondria was abrogated in WAS, ARP2/3-inhibited and ARPC1B-deficient patient MDMs and restored in WAS patients after clinical gene therapy.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: Mitophagy is dependent on the ARP2/3 activity of WASp.
source: This suggests that, as in non-selective autophagy, mitophagy is dependent on the ARP2/3 activity of WASp.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: ARP2/3-dependent actin polymerisation was identified to be important in mitophagic actin cage formation in HEK293 cells in a recent study.
source: Our work here is supported by a recent study where ARP2/3-dependent actin polymerisation was identified to be important in mitophagic actin cage formation in HEK293 cells (Kruppa et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge from a cited reference.

claim: Mitophagic actin cage formation demonstrated in this study bore similarity to the WASp-dependent actin-septin cages seen in a previous study investigating EPEC-mediated xenophagy.
source: Additionally, mitophagic actin cage formation demonstrated in our study here bore similarity to the WASp-dependent actin-septin cages seen in our previous study investigating EPEC-mediated xenophagy (Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a comparison to findings from a previous study by the authors.

claim: This is the first report of an ARP2/3-dependent role for WASp in mitophagy of primary human MDMs.
source: To our knowledge, we are now the first to report an ARP2/3-dependent role for WASp in mitophagy of primary human MDMs.
evidence: This is a statement of the novelty of the study's findings.

claim: A significant disruption to basal mitochondrial morphology was uncovered in WAS MDMs in the absence of mitochondrial insult.
source: Furthermore, in the absence of mitochondrial insult we have surprisingly uncovered a significant disruption to basal mitochondrial morphology in WAS MDMs, suggesting a role for WASp in maintenance of mitochondrial homeostasis.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: It is not clear whether disrupted mitochondrial morphology in the absence of WASp reflects defective mitophagy alone or other as yet unexplored cellular events.
source: Since actin is important in mitochondrial homeostasis through fission and fusion (Li et al., 2015; Hatch et al., 2014; Moore et al., 2016), it is not clear whether disrupted mitochondrial morphology in the absence of WASp reflects defective mitophagy alone or other as yet unexplored cellular events.
evidence: This is a statement acknowledging uncertainty about the mechanism.

claim: The appearance of fragmented mitochondria, as seen in WAS MDMs, has been shown by others to be associated with caspase-1-mediated inflammasome activation in BMDCs.
source: Interestingly, the appearance of fragmented mitochondria, as seen in WAS MDMs, has been shown by others to be associated with caspase-1-mediated inflammasome activation in BMDCs (Park et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge from a cited reference.

claim: Disrupted mitochondrial morphology in WAS could provide a link to inflammasome dysregulation in WAS innate immune cells.
source: This could provide a further link between our findings here of disrupted mitochondrial morphology and previous evidence of inflammasome dysregulation in WAS innate immune cells even in the absence of pathogen challenge (Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation of fragmented mitochondria in WAS and previous findings of inflammasome dysregulation.

claim: Profound defects in mitochondrial respiration were uncovered in WAS MDMs.
source: Exploring the functional consequences of disrupted mitochondrial networks in WAS MDMs uncovered profound defects in mitochondrial respiration.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: Impaired basal mitochondrial respiration in WAS is likely to have a significant impact on cellular functions, through lack of ATP production.
source: Impaired basal mitochondrial respiration in WAS is likely to have a significant impact on cellular functions, through lack of ATP production.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of reduced basal mitochondrial respiration and knowledge of ATP's role in cellular function.

claim: When WASp-deficient MDMs become 'stressed', they are unable to increase their respiratory drive in order to meet the required energy demands.
source: Additionally, we also discovered reduced maximal respiratory capacity, meaning that when WASp-deficient MDMs become 'stressed', they are unable to increase their respiratory drive in order to meet the required energy demands.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Macrophage mitochondria are critical players in the metabolic response to pathogens and cell stress, as they can switch from OxPhos metabolism to glycolysis.
source: Macrophage mitochondria are critical players in the metabolic response to pathogens and cell stress, as they can switch from OxPhos metabolism to glycolysis (O'Neill and Pearce, 2016; Escoll et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge from cited references.

claim: The observed differences in OxPhos in WAS are not explained by an upregulation of glycolysis in WAS.
source: Interestingly, our ECAR analysis revealed that the observed differences in OxPhos are not explained by an upregulation of glycolysis in WAS, with similar rates of glycolysis in healthy donor and WASp-deficient MDMs.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: The discovery of a metabolic defect in WAS MDMs is the first description of its kind.
source: The discovery of a metabolic defect in WAS MDMs is, to our knowledge, the first description of its kind.
evidence: This is a statement of the novelty of the study's findings.

claim: The idea of a metabolic defect in WAS platelets was inferred as early as 40–50 years ago.
source: However, the idea of a metabolic defect in WAS platelets was inferred as early as 40–50 years ago, with several studies observing a paucity of mitochondria and impaired mitochondrial energy production (Trung et al., 1975; Verhoeven et al., 1989; Akkerman et al., 1982; Obydennyi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge from cited references.

claim: Extending metabolic defects to other immune cell lineages may explain other immunophenotypic features of WAS including T cell anergy, progressive reduction in B and T lymphocytes with age and increasing development of autoinflammatory symptoms.
source: Although as yet unstudied, extending these metabolic defects to other immune cell lineages may go some way to explaining other immunophenotypic features of WAS including T cell anergy, progressive reduction in B and T lymphocytes with age and increasing development of autoinflammatory symptoms.
evidence: This is speculation about the broader implications of the study's findings.

claim: Immune cells particularly susceptible to metabolic dysfunction in the presence of impaired autophagy include T regulatory cells, as well as mature T and B cells.
source: This is supported by work in non-WAS models, following emerging evidence of the role of immune cell metabolism in autophagy and differentiation (Clarke and Simon, 2019; Bantug et al., 2018b). Immune cells particularly susceptible to metabolic dysfunction in the presence of impaired autophagy include T regulatory cells, as well as mature T and B cells, which rely more heavily on OxPhos for their differentiation (Clarke and Simon, 2019; Wei et al., 2016; Price et al., 2018; Clarke et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2014; Bantug et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge from cited references.

claim: T regulatory cells, mature T and B cells rely more heavily on OxPhos for their differentiation.
source: This is supported by work in non-WAS models, following emerging evidence of the role of immune cell metabolism in autophagy and differentiation (Clarke and Simon, 2019; Bantug et al., 2018b). Immune cells particularly susceptible to metabolic dysfunction in the presence of impaired autophagy include T regulatory cells, as well as mature T and B cells, which rely more heavily on OxPhos for their differentiation (Clarke and Simon, 2019; Wei et al., 2016; Price et al., 2018; Clarke et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2014; Bantug et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge from cited references.

claim: Human WASp is a key player in both non-selective autophagy and selective mitophagy.
source: Here, we have shown for the first time that human WASp is a key player in both non-selective autophagy and selective mitophagy.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: A significant defect in mitochondrial homeostasis with important metabolic consequences was uncovered in WAS.
source: Moreover, we have uncovered a significant defect in mitochondrial homeostasis with important metabolic consequences and which may have implications well beyond the enhanced inflammatory phenotype of WAS.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: The metabolic defect in WAS may have implications well beyond the enhanced inflammatory phenotype of WAS.
source: Moreover, we have uncovered a significant defect in mitochondrial homeostasis with important metabolic consequences and which may have implications well beyond the enhanced inflammatory phenotype of WAS.
evidence: This is speculation about the broader implications of the study's findings.
